headline: Compose transpose with horizontal reversal
statement: Rotate an n×n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place. Modify the original matrix instead of returning an allocated rotated matrix. The method returns None; the result is the mutation.
intuition: A clockwise rotation can be done in two simple steps. First swap rows and columns by reflecting cells across the main diagonal. Then reverse each row. For example, the old top-left cell ends at the top-right. Both steps change the existing matrix without allocating another matrix.
approach: Transpose by swapping each position above the main diagonal with its mirror.
Reverse each row using two pointers.
Keep the same outer matrix object throughout.
correctness: The transpose places original value (r,c) at (c,r). Row reversal then places it at (c,n-1-r), exactly the clockwise rotation coordinate. Each transpose pair and each row pair is exchanged once, so no value is duplicated or lost.
bruteForce: Allocate a new matrix and assign rotated[col][n-1-row]=matrix[row][col]; this uses O(n²) extra space and violates the in-place requirement.

complexity.explanation: Two passes swap a constant number of values per matrix position without an extra matrix.

pitfalls: Transpose only one side of the diagonal; swapping both sides undoes the transpose.
Reverse rows after transposing for clockwise rotation.
Assigning a new local matrix does not modify the caller’s matrix.
